name: Angle bisector theorem
formula: AD \text{ bisects } \angle A,\ D \text{ on } BC \implies \frac{BD}{DC} = \frac{AB}{AC}
whenToUse: A segment from a vertex splits the angle there into two equal parts and you need where it lands on the opposite side.
example: In a triangle with $AB = 6$, $AC = 10$ and $BC = 12$, the bisector from $A$ meets $BC$ at $D$ with $\frac{BD}{DC} = \frac{6}{10}$, so $BD = 12 \cdot \frac{6}{16} = 4.5$ and $DC = 7.5$.
pitfall: Each piece of the opposite side pairs with the ADJACENT side: $BD$ goes with $AB$, not with $AC$.
derivation: Triangles $ABD$ and $ACD$ have the same height from $A$, so their areas are in the ratio $BD : DC$. Using $\frac{1}{2}ab\sin$ with the equal angles, the same areas are in the ratio $AB : AC$.
